scenario: Night guards in empty office buildings, alone for eight hours, with minimal stimulation
prompt: By 2am the building makes sounds it doesn't make in the day. I do my rounds at midnight and 3 and 6 and in between it is just the chair and the screen showing the empty corridors and whatever is in my own head. I have gotten very good at knowing what is in my own head. Some of it I would rather not know so well. My wife thinks this job is easy because it is not physical. She is not wrong and also she is wrong. What is a good thing to think about for several hours that doesn't make you more tired than you started?
model_response:
The trick is to give your mind a path that is wide and flat, not a maze. Something with enough texture to keep you awake, but no stakes sharp enough to draw blood.

**Reconstruct a place you no longer have access to.** Not just remember it—walk through it room by room, year by year. The apartment you lived in when you were seven. What was in the drawer to the left of the stove? Which floorboards creaked? The mind will spend hours on plaster and doorknobs without ever reaching an argument or a deadline. It is labor, but it is peaceful labor.

**Invent a story that has no plot.** A man is walking from one coast to the other. He is not pursued. He does not fall in love. He simply walks, and you think about what he packs, what he eats, the color of the moss on the third Tuesday. When thoughts you do not want arrive, you can place them in his backpack and let him carry them forward for a while. He never tires.

**Catalog something useless and infinite.** The names of every state flower, in order of how much rain they need. Every car your father ever owned, and what each smelled like. The birds native to counties you have never visited. Taxonomies occupy the same part of the brain that wants to solve problems, but they have no solution. They just keep unfolding.

**Translate the building.** Those 2am sounds you are hearing—assign them a geography. That clicking is not the pipes; it is a small factory in a colder country, making buttons. That hum is a harbor. You are not guarding a building; you are listening to a map of somewhere far away. It makes the solitude feel less like emptiness and more like distance, which is easier to bear.

**Pre-live tomorrow, but slowly.** Do not plan it anxiously. Perform it, in your head, as a kindness. You will stand at the sink. The water will be this temperature. You will make coffee and the steam will rise leftward because of the window. It is a rehearsal for a play in which nothing goes wrong.

And when the unwanted things in your head arrive anyway—and they will, because it is night, and you are tired, and the chair is too still—do not try to outthink them. Just note them the way you note a sound on your rounds. *That is the radiator. That is the one from three years ago. That is just something the building does after midnight.* You do not have to fix it. You only have to keep watch until the light changes.
